concept.name: Commercial paper
concept.definition: Short-term promissory notes issued in bearer form by large corporations, with maturities typically ranging from 5 to 270 days. Because the notes are unsecured, the commercial paper market is generally dominated by large corporations with strong credit ratings.
concept.intuition: Commercial paper is how big, blue-chip companies borrow for a few weeks or months at money-market rates instead of drawing a bank loan.
concept.mechanics: CP is issued at a discount (zero-coupon style) and generally rolls over at maturity, effectively providing continuous working-capital funding. U.S. issues with maturities of 270 days or less are exempt from SEC registration; dealers distribute paper to money market funds and other institutional investors.
concept.failure_modes: Rollover risk is the structural weakness: if the CP market seizes up, as in September 2008, even sound issuers can face a funding cliff. Ratings downgrades can shut an issuer out of the market, and CP is unsecured and not deposit-insured.
concept.misconceptions: That unsecured means broadly unsafe — top-tier CP is among the safest money-market paper, but it still carries issuer default risk and no FDIC insurance. Also, CP is a wholesale institutional instrument, not a retail savings product.
concept.example: A corporation issues $25 million of 90-day commercial paper at a discount to fund seasonal inventory, planning to roll it over at maturity.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
